title: Understanding HTTP & Requests 🌐
description: Learn the basics of HTTP – requests, responses, status codes, and how the web actually works.

slides.title: The Language of the Web
slides.content:
# HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)

Every time you visit a website, your browser sends an **HTTP request** to a server, and the server replies with an **HTTP response**. This is a client‑server protocol – exactly what we'll automate with Python.

* Request: method (GET, POST, etc.), URL, headers, optional body.
* Response: status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found…), headers, body (HTML, JSON, etc.).

slides.title: Common HTTP Methods
slides.content:
# Verbs of the Web

* **GET** – retrieve a resource (page, image, API data).
* **POST** – send data to the server (login form, new comment).
* **PUT** / **PATCH** – update a resource.
* **DELETE** – remove a resource.
* **HEAD** – like GET but only headers, no body.

In hacking, we often send GET to fetch pages, POST to brute‑force logins, and HEAD to probe servers.

quizData.question: Which HTTP method is typically used to submit a login form?
quizData.explanation: POST sends data in the request body, which is standard for form submissions.

slides.title: Status Codes – The Server's Answer
slides.content:
# Three‑Digit Codes

* **2xx** Success: 200 OK, 201 Created.
* **3xx** Redirection: 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found.
* **4xx** Client Error: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found.
* **5xx** Server Error: 500 Internal Server Error.

When you scan a web server, the status code tells you if a resource exists or if you're blocked.

quizData.question: What does a 404 status code mean?
quizData.explanation: 404 means the requested URL does not exist on the server.

slides.title: Headers – Metadata of the Web
slides.content:
# Request and Response Headers

* **User‑Agent** – identifies the client (browser, bot). You can spoof this.
* **Content‑Type** – e.g., `application/json`, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.
* **Cookie** – sends stored cookies back to the server.
* **Set‑Cookie** (response) – tells the client to store a cookie.
* **Authorization** – for sending API keys or tokens.

As a hacker, you'll manipulate headers to impersonate browsers, bypass restrictions, or inject payloads.

slides.title: A Raw HTTP Request (text)
slides.content: What your Python script will send under the hood:
slides.codeSnippet:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (CyberBot)
Accept: text/html

quizData.question: The `User-Agent` header can be set to any string to disguise your script as a different browser.
quizData.explanation: Yes, you can change the User-Agent to mimic different devices or browsers.

slides.title: URL Structure
slides.content:
# scheme://host:port/path?query#fragment

Example: `https://example.com:443/search?q=python#results`

When crafting requests, you'll build URLs dynamically with query parameters.
